course_description: This course will introduce students to foundational social science perspectives on cybercrime, and will examine a number of current and emerging threats that challenge the global security of nation states from a criminological standpoint. Topics to be covered include: social science approaches to and theories of online behaviours, environments, and cyber criminology; human factors in cybercrime commission and victimisation; terrorism and its digital elements; organised crime and its digital components; and cyber warfare, information warfare, and disinformation. Throughout the course, these will be studied in-depth through an examination of specific trends and cases to better understand the level of risk they present. Policy responses will also be canvassed with a focus on the prevention of global security threats, and the regulation of environments, processes, and behaviours that give rise to them.

learning_outcomes.description: Possess a mix of theoretical and applied knowledge related to the social science of online behaviour and online crime.
Possess a mix of theoretical and applied knowledge related to various global security threats and their online elements.
Understand and critically analyse the prevalence and impact of various global security threats.
Understand and critically analyse the strengths and limitations of various policy, prevention, and regulatory responses to global security threats.

The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking.
assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
This assessment item must be submitted via Turnitin on Blackboard Ultra.
Refer to the eLearning Guides for steps on how to submit your Turnitin assignment. No emailed assessments will be accepted. Students must obtain a Digital Receipt as evidence of successful submission of their assessment.
Students must abide by the Student Code of Conduct Policy which outlines that all submitted assessment must be their own work, except where properly referenced.
If you are experiencing technical difficulties with Blackboard or Turnitin, please contact the ITS Support Team .
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 7 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
As these assessments are 48-hours, please be advised that applications for extensions will be considered in line with the intended length of assessment, and so for student equity purposes may result in shorter extensions than other types of assessment.
A request for an extension must be submitted as soon as it becomes evident that an extension is needed, and no later than the assessment due date and time. Please refer to the my.UQ Applying for an assessment extension page for information.
Extension requests are processed by the School of Social Science Administration Team. Course Coordinators are unable to grant extensions directly. Extensions in your final semester of study could delay your graduation to the next graduation period.
Late Extension Applications
Late applications must include supporting documentation outlining how it was impossible, or unsafe, for you to have applied by the due date and time. The School of Social Science will not accept personal statements.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Assessments will not be accepted if it is more than one week (7 calendar days) late without prior approval.
